where status is the code, `no response`, `https only` or `invalid pull request` (`ci.pullRequest`
isn't 1 to 18 digits); no reply body is printed and the exit code
stays as it was.

For `git push` (`accept --push`) the same token goes in `http.extraHeader`, never in a URL:
`Authorization: Basic base64(<user>:<t>)` with user `x-access-token` (`github`), `oauth2` (`gitlab`;
`gitlab-ci-token` when `<t>` is `CI_JOB_TOKEN`), `x-token-auth` (`bitbucket`; a token with `:` is used
as it is).

# Device-frames

# Device frames

| | iOS | Android |
|---|---|---|
| art | Apple's [Product Bezels](https://developer.apple.com/design/resources/#product-bezels) | Android Studio's device art |
| plain | yes | yes |
| App Store (background, title) | yes | no |
| `swiftshot frame <dir>` | yes | no |

On iOS Swiftshot puts screenshots into Apple's official device bezels from Apple's design
resources. It has two modes: plain frames for websites and press kits, and App Store screenshots
with a background and a localized title. Android: see [Android](#android).

![App Store mode in English, German and Arabic, on iPhone 17 Pro Max and iPad Pro 13-inch](images/frames-appstore.png)

```
swiftshot --frame                          # render, then frame (plain)
swiftshot --frame appstore                 # render, then App Store screenshots
swiftshot frame fastlane/screenshots       # frame an existing folder (plain)
swiftshot frame fastlane/screenshots --frame appstore
```

## Modes

### Plain

The device with the screenshot in it, at the bezel's own size, transparent around the device. As
Apple ships it: no shadow, reflection or other effects.

Output: `<output>-framed/<language>/<name>_framed.png`, e.g.
`screenshots-framed/en-US/iPhone 17 Pro Max-Welcome_framed.png`. Use `--frame-output` to change the folder.

Plain frames stay out of the screenshots folder on purpose: they are not App Store sizes and they
have transparency, and `fastlane deliver` checks every image in a language folder.

### App Store

An image at the exact size App Store Connect accepts for the device, with no transparency:

- a background (colour or image),
- an optional keyword and a title, above or below the device,
- the framed device, scaled to fit.

The text never covers the device. Long titles wrap and shrink to fit.

Output: `<output>/<language>/<name>_framed.png`, next to the original.

The canvas is the screenshot's own size when App Store Connect accepts it. Every swiftshot
full-screen capture of a current device is such a size: 1320×2868 for the iPhone 17 Pro Max (6.9"),
2064×2752 for the 13-inch iPad Pro. Otherwise the canvas is the largest accepted size with the
closest aspect ratio.

| Display class | Accepted sizes (portrait; landscape is the same rotated) |
|---|---|
| iPhone 6.9" | 1320×2868, 1290×2796, 1260×2736 |
| iPhone 6.5" | 1284×2778, 1242×2688 |
| iPhone 6.3" | 1206×2622, 1179×2556 |
| iPhone 6.1" | 1170×2532, 1125×2436, 1080×2340 |
| iPhone 5.5" | 1242×2208 |
| iPhone 4.7" | 750×1334 |
| iPhone 4" | 640×1136 |
| iPhone Duo | 1398×2034 (outer), 2007×2853 (inner) |
| iPad 13" | 2064×2752, 2048×2732 |
| iPad 11" | 1668×2420, 1668×2388, 1640×2360, 1488×2266 |
| iPad 10.5" | 1668×2224 |
| iPad 9.7" | 1536×2048 |

Source: [Screenshot specifications](https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/reference/app-information/screenshot-specifications).

Apple Watch screenshots stay unframed in App Store mode: App Store Connect takes the bare screen
(422×514 for Ultra 3). Plain mode frames them.

### What is framed

- Full-screen screenshots, portrait and landscape. Landscape uses Apple's landscape bezel.
- Not partial-size previews (`.sizeThatFitsLayout`, `.fixedLayout`) or `--full-length` captures.
  They are left as they are.
- Devices without an Apple bezel stay unframed. Swiftshot lists them in one warning.

## Options

| Flag | `swiftshot.json` | |
|---|---|---|
| `--frame [plain\|appstore\|none]` | `"frame": "plain"` (or `true`) | Mode. `--frame` alone means plain. |
| `--frame-color <colours>` | `"frame_color"` | Bezel colour: `"Deep Blue"` for every device, `"iPad Pro 13-inch (M5)=Silver"` for one. Comma separated. In JSON a string, a list, or `{"device": "colour"}`. |
| `--framefile <path>` | `"framefile"` | frameit `Framefile.json`. Default: looked up like frameit does (below). |
| `--frame-background <#RRGGBB\|image>` | `"frame_background"` | App Store background. Overrides the Framefile's. |
| `--frame-output <dir>` | `"frame_output"` | Folder for plain frames. Default `<output>-framed`. |
| `--frame-cache <dir>` | `"frame_cache"` | Bezel cache. Default `~/Library/Caches/swiftshot/frames`. |
| `--accept-bezel-license` | `"accept_bezel_license": true` | Accept Apple's license without the prompt (CI). |

`swiftshot frame [<dir>]` takes the same options. `<dir>` defaults to `--output`. It reads device
names from `swiftshot-report.json` when the folder has one, and from the file names otherwise, so it
also frames screenshots from other tools in the deliver layout.

Per screenshot, with the existing `screens` rules:

```
swiftshot --frame appstore --screen "Debug*: frame=none" --screen "Hero: frame=plain"
```

```json
"screens": [{ "preview": "Debug*", "frame": "none" }]
```

## Titles

Swiftshot reads `title.strings` and `keyword.strings` the way frameit does. It looks in the
language folder first, then the screenshots folder, then the folder above it.

```
fastlane/screenshots/en-US/title.strings
"Welcome" = "Build habits that stick";
"Stats" = "See your progress";
"Stats landscape" = "Your week at a glance";
```

- A key matches a screenshot when the file name contains it (ignoring case). The longest matching
  key wins, so `Stats landscape` beats `Stats`.
- Files can be UTF-8 or UTF-16, with or without a byte order mark.
- `\n` in a value starts a new line.
- No text in `.strings` falls back to the Framefile's `title.text` / `keyword.text`.
- No title at all: the device on its background.

Fonts default to the system font (bold for the title), with the language's own fallbacks, so
Arabic, Hebrew, Japanese and so on render correctly and right-to-left text runs right to left.

Defaults without a Framefile:
- background `#F2F2F7` for light screenshots and `#1C1C1E` for dark ones,
- black or white text, whichever contrasts with the background,
- padding 7 % of the short side.

## Framefile.json

Swiftshot reads fastlane frameit's
[Framefile.json](https://docs.fastlane.tools/actions/frameit/#advanced-usage-optional). It looks
for one in the language folder, the screenshots folder and two levels above it, like frameit, unless
`--framefile` names one.

```json
{
  "default": {
    "background": "background.jpg",
    "padding": "6%",
    "title": { "color": "#1D1D1F", "font": "fonts/Inter-Bold.ttf" },
    "keyword": { "color": "#5E5CE6" },
    "stack_title": true
  },
  "data": [
    { "filter": "Stats landscape", "title_below_image": true },
    { "filter": "iPad", "title": { "font_size": 120 } },
    { "filter": "de-DE", "background": "#000000" }
  ]
}
```

Every `data` entry whose `filter` is part of the screenshot's path is merged over `default`, in
file order: later entries win, nested objects merge. The path is relative to the screenshots
folder, e.g. `de-DE/iPad Pro 13-inch (M5)-Stats.png`, so filters can name a language, a device or a
preview. Like frameit, filters are case-sensitive. Relative `font` and `background` paths are
relative to the Framefile.

Supported keys:

| Key | |
|---|---|
| `background` | An image (scaled to fill, centred) or a `#RRGGBB` colour. |
| `title`, `keyword` | `text`, `color` (`#RRGGBB`), `font` (a font file or a font name), `font_size` (pixels), `fonts` (`[{ "font": …, "supported": ["ja", …] }]`, per language). |
| `padding` | Pixels, `"AxB"` (horizontal × vertical) or a percentage of the short side, e.g. `"5%"`. |
| `title_below_image` | Text below the device. |
| `stack_title` | Keyword above the title instead of before it. |
| `show_complete_frame` | `true` (default): the whole device fits. `false`: the device is as wide as the padding allows and runs off the edge away from the text. |
| `title_min_height` | Minimum height of the text area: pixels or a percentage. |
| `font_scale_factor` | Title size as a fraction of the canvas width, when no `font_size` is given. |
| `interline_spacing` | Extra space between lines, in pixels. |
| `frame` | Bezel colour, frameit style (`"BLACK"`, `"SPACE_BLACK"`…). `--frame-color` wins. |

Swiftshot warns about other keys and ignores them, for example `offset`, `use_platform`,
`force_device_type` and `font_weight`.

Differences from frameit:
- `padding` is in output pixels, with no extra factor for @3x devices.
- `show_complete_frame` defaults to `true`.
- The default title size follows the canvas area (about 107 px on 6.9").
- A screenshot without a title is still framed.

## Colours

Names are Apple's. `--frame-color` ignores case, spaces, `-` and `_`. A partial name picks the first
match in alphabetical order (`Natural` picks a natural titanium watch). If a model doesn't have the
colour, swiftshot uses its default and lists the colours it does have.

| Device | Colours (default in bold) |
|---|---|
| iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max | **Black**, Burgundy, Glacier, Silver |
| iPhone 17 Pro, 17 Pro Max | Cosmic Orange, **Deep Blue**, Silver |
| iPhone 17 | **Black**, Lavender, Mist Blue, Sage, White |
| iPhone Air | Cloud White, Light Gold, Sky Blue, **Space Black** |
| iPhone 16 Pro, 16 Pro Max | **Black Titanium**, Desert Titanium, Natural Titanium, White Titanium |
| iPhone 16, 16 Plus | **Black**, Pink, Teal, Ultramarine, White |
| iPhone Duo | **Night Sky**, Star White |
| iPad Pro 11-inch, 13-inch (M5, M4) | Silver, **Space Black** |
| iPad Air 11-inch, 13-inch (M4, M3, M2) | Blue, Purple, **Space Gray**, Starlight |
| iPad mini (A17 Pro) | Blue, Purple, **Space Gray**, Starlight |
| iPad (A16) | Blue, Pink, **Silver**, Yellow |
| Apple Watch Ultra 3 (49mm) | Black or Natural case with an Alpine Loop, Milanese Loop, Ocean Band or Trail Loop, e.g. **Black + Ocean Band Black**, Natural + Trail Loop Green Neon |
| Apple Watch Ultra 2, Ultra (49mm) | Black or Natural with an Alpine Loop, Titanium Milanese Loop, Ocean Band or Trail Loop, e.g. **Black + Ocean Band Black** |
| Apple Watch Series 11, 10 (42mm, 46mm) | Aluminum (Jet Black, Rose Gold, Silver, Space Gray) or Titanium (Gold, Natural, Slate) with a Sport Band, Sport Loop, Milanese Loop or Magnetic Link, e.g. **Aluminum Jet Black + Sport Band Black** |

## Supported devices

The table above. iPad Pro (M4) has the same body and screen as (M5), iPad Air (M2, M3) as (M4),
Apple Watch Series 10 as Series 11, and Apple Watch Ultra as Ultra 2. They use those bezels.

Apple ships no bezels for other devices, for example iPhone 17e, 16e, iPhone 15 and older, iPhone
SE, older iPads and Apple Watch SE. Their screenshots stay unframed and swiftshot says so in one
warning. iPhone Duo is framed with its outer (closed) display.

## fastlane deliver

When a language folder has any `*_framed.png`, `deliver` uploads only the framed files plus the
Apple Watch screenshots, and skips the rest. It then rejects any file that is not an accepted size.
Swiftshot follows that:

- App Store frames are named `<name>_framed.png` next to the originals, so `deliver` uploads them.
- A screenshot that stays unframed in such a folder gets an identical `<name>_framed.png` copy, so
  it is not dropped. That covers a device without a bezel and `frame=none`.
- Plain frames go to their own folder.
- A rendering run removes frames left over from earlier runs, which `deliver` would otherwise
  upload. Frames newer than their screenshot are kept.
- `--clear` deletes images only. `.strings` files and a `Framefile.json` in the language folders
  stay.

## Download and cache

Apple publishes one disk image per family. Most of each image is Photoshop files. Swiftshot
downloads only the families your devices need, once, in parallel and during the build. It mounts
each image read-only, keeps the PNGs, and deletes the image. hdiutil checks the image's checksums.
Swiftshot records each PNG's size and SHA-256 in `manifest.json`, and downloads a family again if a
file is missing or its size changed.

| Family | Download |
|---|---:|
| iPad Pro (M5) | 7 MB |
| iPad mini (A17 Pro) | 8 MB |
| iPad (A16) | 11 MB |
| iPad Air (M4) | 12 MB |
| iPhone 18 | 144 MB |
| Apple Watch Ultra 2 | 186 MB |
| iPhone 17 (17, 17 Pro, 17 Pro Max, Air) | 265 MB |
| iPhone 16 | 273 MB |
| Apple Watch Ultra 3 | 329 MB |
| Apple Watch Series 11 | 358 MB |
| iPhone Duo | 453 MB |

The cache keeps about 2–16 MB of PNGs per family, in `~/Library/Caches/swiftshot/frames/1/`.
On CI, cache that folder:

```yaml
- uses: actions/cache@v6
  with:
    path: ~/Library/Caches/swiftshot/frames
    key: swiftshot-frames-1
- uses: LukasAnda/swiftshot@v0.8.0
  with:
    args: --frame appstore --accept-bezel-license
```

Framing itself is fast. Compositing takes about 6 ms per image; writing the PNG takes most of the
time. On an M4 Pro, 34 frames of an iPhone 17 Pro Max and a 13-inch iPad take 0.9 s.

## Android

```
swiftshot --frame plain
```

```json
{ "frame": "plain" }
```

The device with the screenshot in it, at the art's own size, transparent around the device, with
the screen's rounded corners and camera hole cut out. Plain only: there are no App Store-style
frames, titles or backgrounds on Android, and `--frame` needs the value `plain`.

Output: `<output>-framed/<language>/<name>_framed.png`, e.g.
`screenshots-framed/en-US/Pixel 10 Pro-Welcome-light_framed.png`. With `"layout": "fastlane"` the
`images/<type>Screenshots` folders repeat inside it. The screenshots themselves stay unframed, so
`fastlane supply` uploads the Play sizes.

Only full-screen screenshots get a frame: previews with `showSystemUi = true`, or all with
`--system-ui always`. Components and full-length captures stay unframed.

| devices with art | |
|---|---|
| phones | every Pixel, from Pixel and Pixel XL to Pixel 10 Pro XL, with the a models |
| foldables | Pixel Fold, Pixel 9 Pro Fold, Pixel 10 Pro Fold, unfolded and folded |
| tablets | Pixel Tablet |
| Wear OS | Large Round, Small Round, XL Round, Square, Rectangular |

Other devices, or art whose screen doesn't match the device's size, stay unframed with a warning.

Swiftshot takes the art from, in order:

1. an installed Android Studio (`/Applications`, `~/Applications`, `/opt/android-studio`)
2. the Android SDK's `skins` folder (`ANDROID_HOME`, `ANDROID_SDK_ROOT` or `~/Library/Android/sdk`)
3. [AOSP](https://android.googlesource.com/platform/tools/adt/idea/+/refs/heads/mirror-goog-studio-main/artwork/resources/device-art-resources),
   downloaded once per device into the cache (`~/Library/Caches/swiftshot/android/device-art` on a
   Mac, `~/.cache/swiftshot/android/device-art` on Linux)

WebP art is converted to PNG once. If Java can't read a file, Swiftshot uses `sips` on a Mac,
or ImageMagick or `dwebp` on Linux.

The device art is part of Android Studio and licensed under the Apache License 2.0.

## License

The bezels are Apple's. Swiftshot does not include or redistribute them: it downloads them from
Apple on your machine. They come under the
[Apple Design Resources License](https://developer.apple.com/support/downloads/terms/apple-design-resources/Apple-Design-Resources-License-20230621-English.pdf),
which you accept once, at the prompt or with `--accept-bezel-license`. Use the frames as Apple's
[marketing guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/marketing/guidelines/) describe.
Plain mode keeps the bezels as Apple ships them.

# Migrating-from-fastlane

# Migrating

From fastlane snapshot and screengrab, Paparazzi and Roborazzi.

- [fastlane snapshot (iOS)](#fastlane-snapshot-ios)
- [fastlane screengrab (Android)](#fastlane-screengrab-android)
- [Paparazzi and Roborazzi](#paparazzi-and-roborazzi)

## fastlane snapshot (iOS)

### What changes

| fastlane snapshot | swiftshot |
|---|---|
| UI test target, `SnapshotHelper.swift`, `snapshot("name")` calls | your existing `#Preview`s |
| launch arguments to navigate to each screen | none, each preview is a screen |
| `Snapfile` | `swiftshot.json` |
| a booted simulator per device | no simulator |
| a UI test session per device and language | one app process per language |

The output layout is the same, so `fastlane deliver` and `frameit` keep working.

### Snapfile keys

| Snapfile | swiftshot.json |
|---|---|
| `project` / `workspace` | `project` / `workspace` |
| `scheme` | `scheme` (the app scheme, not the UI test scheme) |
| `devices` | `devices` |
| `languages` | `languages` |
| `ios_version` | `ios_versions` |
| `dark_mode` | `appearances: ["dark"]` |
| `output_directory` | `output_directory` |
| `clear_previous_screenshots` | `clear_previous_screenshots` |
| `override_status_bar` | `status_bar` (on by default) |
| `skip_open_summary` | not needed, swiftshot never opens the summary (`html: false` is not the same: it removes the HTML files, `index.html` of a verify report too) |
| `concurrent_simulators` | not needed |
| `launch_arguments` | set state in the preview |
| `erase_simulator`, `reinstall_app` | not needed |

### Steps

1. Make sure each screen you capture has a `#Preview`, with the sample data it needs.
2. Run `swiftshot init`, then compare its `swiftshot.json` with your `Snapfile`.
3. Run `swiftshot` and review `screenshots/screenshots.html`.
4. Add the [fastlane plugin](https://github.com/LukasAnda/fastlane-plugin-swiftshot)
   (`fastlane add_plugin swiftshot`) and replace `capture_ios_screenshots` / `snapshot` in your
   lane with `swiftshot`. It takes the same `devices`, `languages`, `dark_mode`,
   `output_directory` and `clear_previous_screenshots`:
   `swiftshot(devices: ["iPhone 17 Pro Max"], languages: ["en-US", "de-DE"])`
5. Delete the UI test target and `SnapshotHelper.swift` if nothing else uses them.

Preview names become screenshot names: `#Preview("01 Welcome")` gives `<device>-01 Welcome.png`,
which keeps App Store order.

## fastlane screengrab (Android)

### What changes

| fastlane screengrab | swiftshot |
|---|---|
| instrumentation tests, `Screengrab.screenshot("name")` calls | your existing `@Preview`s |
| `androidTest` APK, Espresso or UI Automator to reach each screen | none, each preview is a screen |
| `Screengrabfile` | `swiftshot.json` |
| a running emulator or device | no emulator |
| `assembleDebug` and `assembleAndroidTest` | one Gradle task, the debug variant |

In a lane, `swiftshot(platform: "android", languages: ["en-US", "de-DE"])` from the
[fastlane plugin](https://github.com/LukasAnda/fastlane-plugin-swiftshot) replaces
`capture_android_screenshots` and writes the supply layout by default.

With `"layout": "fastlane"`, the output is where `fastlane supply` uploads from:
`metadata/android/<locale>/images/phoneScreenshots`, `sevenInchScreenshots`,
`tenInchScreenshots`, `tvScreenshots` and `wearScreenshots`.

### Screengrabfile keys

| Screengrabfile | swiftshot.json |
|---|---|
| `app_package_name`, `tests_package_name` | not needed; `modules` picks the Gradle modules |
| `app_apk_path`, `tests_apk_path` | not needed, Swiftshot builds `variant` |
| `locales` | `languages` |
| `output_directory` | `output_directory` with `"layout": "fastlane"` |
| `clear_previous_screenshots` | `clear_previous_screenshots` |
| `device_type` (`phone`, `sevenInch`, `tenInch`, `tv`, `wear`) | `devices`, `watch_devices`; the folder follows the device |
| `specific_device` | not needed |
| `use_tests_in_classes`, `use_tests_in_packages` | `previews` or `screens` with `skip` |
| `launch_arguments` | set state in the preview |
| `skip_open_summary` | not needed, swiftshot never opens the summary (`html: false` is not the same: it removes the HTML files, `index.html` of a verify report too) |
| `use_timestamp_suffix` | not needed, names are stable |
| `reinstall_app`, `exit_on_test_failure` | not needed |

### Steps

1. Make sure each screen you capture has a `@Preview` with `showSystemUi = true` and the sample
   data it needs, and the module has `debugImplementation("androidx.compose.ui:ui-tooling")`.
2. Run `swiftshot init`. With a `fastlane` folder it sets
   `"output_directory": "fastlane/metadata/android"` and `"layout": "fastlane"`.
3. Run `swiftshot` and review `fastlane/metadata/android/screenshots.html`.
4. Replace `capture_android_screenshots` / `screengrab` in your lane:
   `sh("swiftshot run --config ../swiftshot.json")`
5. Delete the screenshot tests and the screengrab dependency if nothing else uses them.

`supply` uploads every image in an `images/<type>Screenshots` folder, in name order. Render one
appearance for upload (`"appearances": ["light"]` or `["dark"]`), and name previews in the order
you want: `@Preview(name = "01 Welcome", showSystemUi = true)` gives
`Pixel 10 Pro-01 Welcome.png`.

## Paparazzi and Roborazzi

Swiftshot renders `@Preview`s with layoutlib, the renderer Paparazzi uses (Roborazzi renders with
Robolectric), so a screenshot test that calls a previewed composable can be replaced by the preview,
on the same device and settings.

Run `swiftshot init` in the project. It never runs Gradle and removes nothing: Paparazzi and
Roborazzi stay in the project, and only `swiftshot.json` and `swiftshot-migration.md` are written.

### What init reads

- Modules that use either tool: the plugin, a version-catalog alias, a convention plugin
  (`build-logic`, `buildSrc`, included builds) or test imports.
- Each test's device: Paparazzi `DeviceConfig` presets and custom configs, Robolectric and
  Roborazzi qualifier strings (`@Config(qualifiers = ...)`, `setQualifiers`),
  `RobolectricDeviceQualifiers` and `robolectric.properties`. A device it can't read is reported,
  never guessed.
- Languages, only what the tests set. If none do, `en-US`, and the app's other string-resource
  languages are listed for you to add.

### What it writes

A `screens` rule per tested preview (by fully qualified function), so each preview renders only
on the devices and settings of its tests (`override_preview` where a test replaces the preview's
own). A final rule skips the previews no test covers. See [[Configuration]].

### swiftshot-migration.md

The same report is printed and saved. It lists:

- the modules found and the device each test uses (labelled "tool default", "from @Preview" or
  "unresolved" when it was not read from the test)
- tests without a matching `@Preview` (add a `@Preview` with the same arguments to include them),
  and tests it couldn't read
- previews whose screenshot size differs from the old tool's (Paparazzi renders the full screen;
  Swiftshot crops to the content unless the `@Preview` sets `showSystemUi`)
- previews no test covers, which are skipped

### Side by side

Keep the Paparazzi or Roborazzi tests while you check the output, and delete them when you are
ready.

### Baselines

Swiftshot doesn't compare images yet (planned for 1.0.0). Its first baseline will come from CI,
not from the images Paparazzi or Roborazzi recorded, because the renderer differs.

# How-it-works

On iOS, Swiftshot runs your simulator app as a plain Mac process, gives it a virtual screen with
the target device's exact geometry, and lets Core Animation render each preview into it. No
simulator is created or booted. This page explains each step and how the output is kept identical
to a booted simulator. On Android, it renders Compose previews with layoutlib, the engine of
Android Studio's previews, in parallel processes: see [Android](#android). Flutter previews
render with `flutter test`, or on Flutter's iOS engine: see [Flutter](#flutter).

- [Overview](#overview)
- [1. Build once](#1-build-once)

## Overview

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    CLI["swiftshot"] -->|"xcodebuild, once"| APP["MyApp.app<br/>simulator build, Debug"]
    APP --> FAN{"one job per<br/>device × language,<br/>in parallel"}
    FAN --> P1["simhost → MyApp process<br/>iPhone 17 Pro Max · en-US"]
    FAN --> P2["simhost → MyApp process<br/>iPhone 17 Pro Max · de-DE"]
    FAN --> P3["simhost → MyApp process<br/>iPad Pro 13-inch · en-US"]
    P1 -->|"every preview ×<br/>appearance × text size"| OUT[("screenshots/&lt;lang&gt;/*.png<br/>screenshots.html<br/>swiftshot-report.json")]
    P2 --> OUT
    P3 --> OUT
```

The jobs run in parallel, up to half the Mac's cores. A job starts in about a second and then
renders each screenshot in well under a second.

## 1. Build once

Swiftshot runs one `xcodebuild build` for the iOS simulator (`arm64`, no code signing) and reads
the `.app` path from the build settings. The same build serves every device, iOS version and
language. It must be a Debug build, because the compiler only includes `#Preview` code in Debug.
`--app` skips the build and uses a prebuilt `.app`.

## 2. Launch without a simulator

A simulator app is an ordinary arm64 Mac binary linked against the simulator runtime's
frameworks. It runs as a normal process once it gets what `launchd_sim` in a booted simulator
would give it, plus the services a booted device provides.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    SH["<b>swiftshot-simhost</b><br/>Mac program"]
    RT[("Simulator<br/>runtime")]
    subgraph PROC["MyApp process: the simulator binary, run directly on the Mac"]
        direction TB
        AG["<b>swiftshot agent</b><br/>finds previews · fakes device geometry<br/>status bar · capture"]
        A["your previews"]
        UI["UIKit · SwiftUI"]
        CA["Core Animation render server<br/>(in-process)"]
        FD["<b>virtual display</b><br/>replaces SimFramebufferClient"]
        SHIM["<b>NoBoot shim</b><br/>routes system XPC to simhost"]
        AG --> A --> UI --> CA --> FD
        CA -.- SHIM
    end
    SH -->|"starts app,<br/>injects agent + shim"| AG
    SHIM <-.->|"Metal · IOSurface ·<br/>shader compiler"| SH
    RT -.->|"frameworks"| UI
    FD -->|"IOSurface"| PNG[("PNG")]
```

**Environment.** The CLI sets what a booted device's launchd would: `SIMULATOR_ROOT` and
`IPHONE_SIMULATOR_ROOT` pointing at the runtime's `RuntimeRoot`, a fresh `HOME` and `TMPDIR` per
job, and the device variables (`SIMULATOR_MODEL_IDENTIFIER`, `SIMULATOR_CAPABILITIES`,
`SIMULATOR_MAINSCREEN_WIDTH/HEIGHT/SCALE`, …). The language is passed as `-AppleLanguages` and
`-AppleLocale`, as on a device.

**swiftshot-simhost** is a small Mac program that starts the app. It sets the `DYLD_*` variables
itself, because System Integrity Protection strips them from anything started through a system
binary:

- `DYLD_ROOT_PATH` loads every framework from the simulator runtime instead of macOS.
- `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` injects the NoBoot shim and the swiftshot agent.
- `DYLD_SHARED_CACHE_DIR` points at the runtime's dyld cache. Swiftshot builds that cache once if
  the runtime has none.

It also turns off the crash reporter for the child, so a crashing preview never opens a dialog.

**Services.** In a booted simulator, Metal, IOSurface and the shader compiler are XPC services
that CoreSimulator provides from the Mac. simhost provides the same three itself, using the
Mac's own private implementations (`MTLSimImplementation.framework` and `IOSurfaceRemoteServer`).
Each shader compile request gets a new `MTLCompilerService` from the runtime. simhost hands the
services to the app as registered Mach ports.

**NoBoot shim.** The shim intercepts `xpc_connection_create_mach_service` and
`xpc_connection_create` inside the app. Connections to `com.apple.metal.simulator*`,
`com.apple.IOSurface.Remote` and `com.apple.MTLCompilerService` go to simhost's ports. Everything
else passes through unchanged.

**Agent start.** The agent's constructor runs before the app's `main`. It creates the
`UIApplication` by hand and starts rendering. The app's own `@main` and scene setup never run, so
only the previews are rendered.

## 3. Find the previews

`#Preview` expands to a type that conforms to `PreviewRegistry` (from `DeveloperToolsSupport`).
Legacy previews conform to `PreviewProvider`. The agent finds both the way the Swift runtime
finds protocol conformances:

1. Walk the `__TEXT,__swift5_proto` section of every image in the app bundle.
2. Keep the records that conform to `PreviewRegistry` or `PreviewProvider`.
3. Call each type's metadata accessor to get the type, then `makePreview()`.
4. Read the display name, traits (orientation, `.sizeThatFitsLayout`, `.fixedLayout`) and the body
   closure from the result.

Previews are ordered by file and line. Unnamed previews are called `<File>_<line>`.
`swiftshot list` prints what was found.

## 4. Pretend to be the device

UIKit asks the screen, the device and MobileGestalt what it runs on. The agent answers every
question with the target device's measured values:

| what | how |
|---|---|
| screen size, scale, corner radii | `UIScreen` getters, from the device type's `capabilities.plist` |
| idiom (phone, pad) | `UIDevice.userInterfaceIdiom` |
| safe areas, Dynamic Island area | `_UIDisplayInfoProvider` getters and `UIScreen._exclusionArea`, from the [device table](#11-device-table) |
| status bar height and axis | `UIStatusBarManager` getters |
| size classes, display scale, P3 gamut, layout direction | trait overrides on the window |
| large-phone content margins | the MobileGestalt answer for that model |

That's also why each device model gets its own process: some of these values are read once per
process.

## 5. Render and capture

**Virtual display.** UIKit draws through Core Animation, which on a simulator presents frames to
the simulator's framebuffer through `SimFramebufferClient`. The agent replaces that framework's
functions with a virtual display. It reports the device's exact display modes and shows every
swap like a booted simulator's display: a frame that redrew only part of the screen updates
only that rect. With `CA_FORCE_LOCAL_SERVER=1`, the Core Animation render
server (`CAWindowServer`) runs inside the app process, and the app's window is hosted into it
with a `CALayerHost`, the way SpringBoard hosts apps.

**Deterministic rendering.** Three render server options are pinned, because without them pixels
depend on the machine's speed:

| option | without it |
|---|---|
| `CA_DISABLE_GENERIC_SHADERS` | the first frames use a generic shader while the specialized one compiles, so glass differs with compile speed |
| `CA_DISABLE_OCCLUSION_CULLING` | antialiased edges depend on what the reused display buffers held before |
| `CA_DISABLE_SDF_CACHE` | glass edges freeze as first drawn, depending on frame timing |

**Capture.**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Agent as swiftshot agent
    participant UI as UIKit / SwiftUI
    participant RS as Render server (in-process)
    participant FB as Virtual display
    Agent->>UI: put the preview in a device-sized window
    Agent->>RS: purge cached resources
    Agent->>RS: commit window, status bar and root in one transaction
    Agent->>RS: waitForCommitId
    RS->>FB: render and present the frame
    loop until 3 identical frames (5 if any two differed, at most 12)
        Agent->>RS: force a redraw (no visible change)
        RS->>FB: present
        FB-->>Agent: newest IOSurface
    end
    Agent->>Agent: write the PNG
```

Each redraw damages the frame without changing what it shows, so a frame that's still settling
(an animation, glass adapting to the content behind it) shows up as a difference. iOS 26 also
waits for its glass brightness loop to go quiet. On iOS 27 iPhones with a Dynamic Island, the
server then redraws the rect SpringBoard's system aperture redraws on a device once an app is
up (from the top-left corner to just past the island), as partial frames: a blurred backdrop cut
by that rect comes out a step different inside it, as on the device. Previews that aren't full screen are rendered
over black and over white, and the alpha channel is computed from the two.

## 6. Status bar

Full-screen shots use the status bar component SpringBoard itself uses (`STUIStatusBar` from
`SystemStatusUI.framework`). It gets the same data `simctl status_bar override` sets: 9:41, full
Wi-Fi and cellular signal, and a charged battery. It's laid out around the Dynamic Island,
picks light or dark from the content under it like on a device, and follows the device language
for direction and digits. It lives in its own window above the app. `--no-status-bar` leaves it
out.

## 7. Previews, sheets and options

| feature | how |
|---|---|
| Sheets, alerts, dialogs | animations are turned off, so presentations land in their final state before capture |
| `.sizeThatFitsLayout` | measured with `sizeThatFits`; no safe area |
| `.fixedLayout(width:height:)` | rendered at that size |
| landscape traits | landscape window, safe areas and size classes |
| `--full-length` | the window grows to the largest scroll view's content, up to 16384 px |
| text sizes | a `preferredContentSizeCategory` override per screenshot |
| dark mode | `overrideUserInterfaceStyle` per screenshot |
| languages | one process per language, started with `-AppleLanguages` and `-AppleLocale`; right-to-left layout for RTL languages |
| UIKit previews | `UIViewController` and `UIView` bodies are hosted directly |

## 8. Apple Watch

watchOS previews use the same approach. The app runs without a simulator, the agent answers
`UIScreen` and `WKInterfaceDevice` with the watch's geometry, and each preview is hosted in a
window on the in-process render server. One process runs per model, text size and language.

## 9. Device mode, the reference

`--mode device` renders the same previews in real booted simulators, and is what no-boot output
is checked against.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant CLI as swiftshot CLI
    participant Sim as Booted simulator
    participant Agent as agent in the app
    CLI->>Sim: create, boot, install, status_bar override
    CLI->>Sim: simctl launch (agent injected)
    Agent->>Sim: pin the same three render options
    Agent->>CLI: launch.ready
    CLI->>CLI: wait until SpringBoard hides the home indicator
    CLI->>Agent: launch.done
    loop every screenshot
        Agent->>Agent: show the preview
        Agent->>CLI: N.ready
        CLI->>Sim: simctl io screenshot, until two grabs match
        CLI->>Agent: N.done
    end
```

The agent and the CLI talk through files in a shared folder. If the home indicator never hides or
a screenshot command hangs, the simulator is rebooted and the run is repeated, up to 3 times. On
machines with little memory, simulators take turns.

## 10. Proving it's pixel identical

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    DEMO["Example/DemoApp"] --> NB["no-boot render"]
    DEMO --> D1["--mode device, run 1"]
    DEMO --> D2["--mode device, run 2"]
    NB --> CMP{"every pixel equal<br/>to run 1 or run 2?"}
    D1 --> CMP
    D2 --> CMP
    CMP -->|"yes"| PASS["pass"]
    CMP -->|"any pixel off"| FAIL["fail"]
```

The integration tests render the demo app both ways and require a difference of 0 on every pixel
of every channel. The booted simulator itself flips a few glass pixels by 1/255 between runs, so
each pixel may match either of two device runs. The tests cover iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 17,
iPad Pro 13-inch, iPhone Duo and Apple Watch, with sheets, alerts, glass and the status bar.
Other tests check that two no-boot runs are byte-identical, that no simulator gets booted, and
a time budget per screenshot.

## 11. Device table

Screen size, scale and corner radii come from each device type's `capabilities.plist` in Xcode.
Safe areas, the Dynamic Island area and status bar metrics can only be measured on a booted
device. `swiftshot calibrate` boots each device once and records them, and the results ship
inside swiftshot. A weekly workflow measures any device type the table doesn't have yet on the
GitHub runners and opens a pull request, so new devices work without booting anything on your
machine.

## Why it's faster than fastlane

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph SS["swiftshot"]
        direction TB
        S1["build app"] --> S2["for each device × language, in parallel:<br/>start one process (~1 s)"]
        S2 --> S3["for each preview: render one frame"]
    end
    subgraph FL["fastlane snapshot"]
        direction TB
        F1["build app + UI tests"] --> F2["for each device: boot simulator"]
        F2 --> F3["for each language: install test runner,<br/>launch the app"]
        F3 --> F4["for each screen: relaunch,<br/>tap to the screen, wait, capture"]
    end
```

| | fastlane snapshot | swiftshot |
|---|---|---|
| builds | app and UI tests | app |
| simulators booted | one per device | none |
| app launches | one per screen, device and language | one per device and language |
| getting to a screen | XCUITest taps | the preview is the screen |
| per screenshot, free GitHub runner | 93 s | 1.2–2.2 s, build included |

## Android

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    CLI["swiftshot"] -->|"init script"| G["Gradle<br/>swiftshotPrepare"]
    G -->|"module.json:<br/>classes, classpath,<br/>resources, assets"| SCAN["@Preview scan<br/>(bytecode)"]
    SCAN --> PLAN["groups:<br/>device × language ×<br/>appearance × font scale"]
    PLAN --> R1["renderer 1<br/>layoutlib"]
    PLAN --> R2["renderer 2<br/>layoutlib"]
    PLAN --> RN["renderer n<br/>layoutlib"]
    R1 --> OUT[("PNGs, gallery,<br/>report, frames")]
    R2 --> OUT
    RN --> OUT
```

**Build.** Swiftshot runs `./gradlew -I <init script> swiftshotPrepare -Pswiftshot.variant=debug`.
The init script adds the task to every Android application and library module for this one
invocation; nothing in the project changes. The task compiles the variant as usual, resolves its
runtime classpath together with Paparazzi's layoutlib SDK, and writes the module's classes,
classpath, resources and assets to `build/intermediates/swiftshot/<variant>/module.json`. The
task holds no reference to the project and the script sits at a fixed path in the cache, so the
project's configuration cache stays valid: a warm Gradle step takes about a second.

**Find previews.** `@Preview` has binary retention, so reflection can't see it. Swiftshot reads
the compiled class files with ASM and resolves multipreview annotations (`@PreviewLightDark`,
`@WearPreviewDevices`, your own) through the project's classes and its libraries.

**Render.** Each renderer is a JVM with the app's classpath and layoutlib, loaded through
Paparazzi's SDK. It inflates Compose's own `ComposeViewAdapter`, as Android Studio does, so
`@PreviewParameter`, inspection mode and the preview wrappers behave as in the IDE. A process
starts once and then renders whole groups of screenshots that share a device, language,
appearance and font scale, swapping only the composable. Groups go to whichever process is free.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant CLI as swiftshot
    participant G as Gradle
    participant R as renderer processes
    CLI->>R: start, with the previous run's classpath
    CLI->>G: swiftshotPrepare
    R->>R: load layoutlib, apply its patches
    G-->>CLI: module.json
    CLI->>CLI: scan previews, plan groups
    alt classpath unchanged
        CLI->>R: send groups
    else classpath changed
        CLI->>R: start new processes, send groups
    end
    R-->>CLI: one line per screenshot
    CLI->>R: stop
```

Renderer processes start while Gradle builds, and are used when the classpath comes out the
same. The first process writes a class-data-sharing archive of the classpath, which makes every
later start faster. Several processes run in parallel: one per core and 1.5 GB of memory, at most
8, or `--parallel`.

**System bars.** On a device the status bar and gesture handle are system windows above the app
(and above a dialog's scrim). Apps that target API 35 or later are edge-to-edge, so the content
gets the device's real insets (a status bar sized to the camera cutout, the gesture area at the
bottom) and draws behind them. Swiftshot then draws the bars over the finished frame: 9:30, full
Wi-Fi, signal and battery, and the gesture handle. Older apps keep layoutlib's own bars.

**Wear OS.** Watch devices render with the watch UI mode and, for round screens, a round screen
configuration. Wear OS has no light mode, so they render once, dark. Outside the circle the image
is black (Play rejects transparency), or transparent with `round_corners`.

**Full length.** With `full_length`, Swiftshot reads how far the preview's vertical scroll
containers can still scroll from Compose's semantics (the vertical scroll range that
`verticalScroll` and `LazyColumn` report), grows the screen by that much and renders again, until
nothing scrolls.

**Encoding.** PNG encoding, and framing, run on separate threads beside the next render, at a
fast deflate level instead of ImageIO's slowest one.

### Why it's faster than Paparazzi and Roborazzi

They run screenshots as unit tests: Gradle compiles a test source set, and a test task renders
one screenshot per test, one at a time per JVM. Swiftshot has no test sources to compile and no
test task, and keeps parallel renderers up for the whole run.

The same 470 screenshots on a free 4-core `ubuntu-latest` runner
([`bench/android`](https://github.com/LukasAnda/swiftshot/tree/main/bench/android)):

| | swiftshot | Paparazzi 2.0.0-alpha05.1 | Roborazzi 1.77.0 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| first run | **59.4 s** | 86.8 s | 87.7 s |
| warm run | **36.7 s** | 63.6 s | 70.2 s |

## Compose Multiplatform

A multiplatform module is prepared per target by the same init script:

- **Android** (`com.android.library` or `com.android.kotlin.multiplatform.library`): layoutlib,
  as above, labelled `:shared (android)`.
- **Desktop** (the first `jvm()` target): Compose's own `ImageComposeScene`, rendered by Skia
  headless, with no window.
- **iOS** (`iosSimulatorArm64()`): previews are found on the JVM target. The init script adds a
  `SwiftshotHost` framework with a generated wrapper per preview (`ComposeUIViewController`);
  private previews are made internal in copies of the sources. A small SwiftUI host app gets a
  `#Preview` per preview, and the iOS no-boot renderer renders it as it does any app.

Component previews (no `showSystemUi`) render on iOS at the size the desktop renderer measured.
The iOS output is pixel identical to a booted simulator (checked on iPhone 17 Pro Max and iPad
Pro 13-inch, light and dark, left to right and right to left).

## Flutter

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    CLI["swiftshot"] --> S["find every @Preview<br/>(lib/, no build)"]
    S --> H["flutter test<br/>one process per language"]
    S -->|"Mac with Xcode"| I["Flutter bundle for the simulator<br/>in a SwiftUI host app"]
    I --> R["iOS no-boot renderer"]
    H & R --> OUT[("PNG per preview,<br/>device, language, appearance")]
```

1. Swiftshot reads the `@Preview`s from the Dart sources in `lib/`, without building, and
   generates a test file per language that imports them.
2. **Headless.** `flutter test` renders each preview with Impeller (Skia as a fallback), with
   the previewer's layers (wrapper, theme, size, brightness, text scale, localizations) in a
   `MaterialApp`, at the device's size, scale and safe areas. Each language gets its own process
   and fonts. Full screens get system bars drawn over the frame, as on Android.
3. **Exact iOS.** On a Mac with Xcode, iPhones and iPads render on Flutter's iOS engine instead:
   `flutter build ios --simulator` builds the app's Flutter bundle (skipped when nothing
   changed), a generated SwiftUI host app gets a `#Preview` per preview, and the no-boot iOS
   renderer renders it like any app. The status bar is the system's own; components render at
   their declared size, or the size the headless pass measured.

The exact iOS output is pixel identical to a booted simulator, and every run is byte identical.

# Troubleshooting

Run with `--verbose` for the full log. `swiftshot-report.json` in the output folder lists every
screenshot, timings and errors.

## iOS

**No previews found.** Build with the Debug configuration; `#Preview` code is left out of Release
builds. `swiftshot list` prints what was found.

**A runtime isn't installed.** Install it in Xcode > Settings > Components, or pass
`--download-missing-runtimes`. `swiftshot devices` lists what's installed.

**A device is skipped.** Each runtime supports only some devices. Pick a runtime that supports it,
or pass `--allow-unsupported-devices` to render it anyway (best effort).

**Images or animations are not finished.** Load sample data synchronously in the preview, or pass
`--delay <seconds>` (per screen: `delay`).

**A long list is cut off.** Use `--full-length` or `"full_length": true` for that screen.

**The watch app isn't rendered.** Add a watch model to `devices` and set `watch_scheme` if the
watch app has its own scheme.

**A launch times out.** The default limit is 600 s; raise it with `--timeout`.

## Android

**No JDK 21.** `swiftshot needs a JDK 21 or later` (from the launcher) or `Swiftshot needs JDK 21
or later to render Android previews`: install one (`openjdk-21-jre-headless` on Debian and Ubuntu,
`java-21-openjdk-headless` on Fedora), or set `JAVA_HOME`, `SWIFTSHOT_JAVA_HOME` or `--java-home`.
Android Studio's JDK and the ones in `/usr/lib/jvm` are found automatically. The lookup order is
on [[Installation]].

**ui-tooling missing.** `:app has no androidx.compose.ui:ui-tooling on its debug classpath; add
debugImplementation("androidx.compose.ui:ui-tooling") as Android Studio's previews need it too.`
Add that line to the module's dependencies. With `--variant`, the dependency must be on that
variant's classpath.

**iOS runs instead of Android.** A folder with an `.xcodeproj` or `.xcworkspace`, or a
`swiftshot.json` with `project`, `workspace` or `scheme`, is an iOS project. Pass
`--platform android`, or `--project-dir` to point at the Gradle project.

**iOS needs a Mac.** `iOS needs a Mac with Xcode` on Linux: `--platform ios`, a folder with an
Xcode project, `swiftshot frame`, `calibrate` and `emit-table` need the Mac tool. In a Compose
Multiplatform project the iOS targets are skipped and the rest renders.

**A note about iOS keys.** `swiftshot.json: scheme, mode are for iOS on a Mac; ignored here`: the
file is shared with the iOS tool. Nothing to fix.

**Gradle failed.** `Gradle failed (exit <n>)` is followed by the last 40 lines of Gradle's
output; `--verbose` shows all of it. Run `./gradlew assembleDebug` to see whether the project
builds on its own. Pass extra Gradle arguments with `--gradle-arg` (repeatable) or `gradle_args`.
`Could not resolve app.cash.paparazzi:paparazzi` or `com.android.tools.layoutlib`: add
`mavenCentral()` to the project's repositories.

**Configuration cache.** Swiftshot keeps the project's configuration cache: its init script stays
at one path in the cache folder and its task holds no reference to the project. If Gradle still
reports configuration cache problems, run with `--gradle-arg=--no-configuration-cache` and open an
issue.

**No previews found.** `No @Preview functions found in …`: the module compiled no `@Preview`
functions in that variant. `swiftshot list` prints what was found, per module.

**Unknown device.** `` Unknown device "…". `swiftshot devices` lists them. `` Use a name or id from
`swiftshot devices`, or a `*` glob. `<preview>: unknown device "…"` means a `@Preview(device = …)`
that isn't in Android Studio's catalog; use `Devices.*`, `id:…` or `spec:…`.

**Not framed.** `No device art for pixel_9 (…)`: the device art could not be found locally or
downloaded from AOSP. Install Android Studio, or run once with network access so it lands in the
cache; offline CI can restore the cache folder ([[CI]]). Devices without art stay unframed.

**Wear OS renders dark only.** Wear OS has no light mode, so watch screens render once, dark,
with no appearance suffix. A preview's own `uiMode` still wins.

**`apiLevel` is ignored.** Every preview renders with layoutlib's Android version.

**A long list is cut off.** Use `--full-length` or `"full_length": true` for that screen. It grows
the screen while Compose reports more to scroll (`verticalScroll`, `LazyColumn`).

**Animations or images are not finished.** `--delay <seconds>` advances the preview's clock before
capture. Load sample data synchronously in the preview.

## Something else

[Open an issue](https://github.com/LukasAnda/swiftshot/issues/new/choose) with `swiftshot
--version`, the command and the log, and `xcodebuild -version` (iOS) or `./gradlew --version`
(Android).

# Roadmap

What's planned for upcoming versions. Version numbers are targets and can move. Each version has a
[milestone](https://github.com/LukasAnda/swiftshot/milestone) that tracks its work.
[Open a feature request](https://github.com/LukasAnda/swiftshot/issues/new?template=feature_request.yml)
to suggest something or to say what you need most.

| version | | status |
|---|---|---|
| [v0.3.0](https://github.com/LukasAnda/swiftshot/releases/tag/v0.3.0) | [Homebrew](#v030--homebrew) | released |
| [v0.4.0](https://github.com/LukasAnda/swiftshot/releases/tag/v0.4.0) | [Android: Jetpack Compose](#v040--android-jetpack-compose) | released |
| [v0.5.0](https://github.com/LukasAnda/swiftshot/releases/tag/v0.5.0) | [Compose Multiplatform](#v050--compose-multiplatform) | released |
| [v0.6.0](https://github.com/LukasAnda/swiftshot/releases/tag/v0.6.0) | [Linux as a full host](#v060--linux-as-a-full-host) | released |
| [v0.7.0](https://github.com/LukasAnda/swiftshot/releases/tag/v0.7.0) | [Flutter](#v070--flutter) | released |
| [v0.8.0](https://github.com/LukasAnda/swiftshot/releases/tag/v0.8.0) | [Migration from Paparazzi and Roborazzi](#v080--migration-from-paparazzi-and-roborazzi) | released |
| 1.0.0 | [Baseline comparison](#v100--baseline-comparison) | next |

## v0.3.0 · Homebrew

`brew install lukasanda/tap/swiftshot`, with updates through `brew upgrade`. The formula is
in [LukasAnda/homebrew-tap](https://github.com/LukasAnda/homebrew-tap) and every release
updates it. The GitHub Action and the install script stay.

## v0.4.0 · Android: Jetpack Compose

Screenshots of `@Preview` composables for phones, foldables, tablets and Wear OS, every locale,
font scale and dark mode, from one command, on a Mac or Linux. See [[Android]].

## v0.5.0 · Compose Multiplatform

Shared `@Preview`s rendered for Android, desktop and iOS from one configuration, so a
multiplatform app gets Play Store, desktop and App Store screenshots in one run. See
[[Compose Multiplatform]].

## v0.6.0 · Linux as a full host

The same `swiftshot` command, `swiftshot init` and configuration on Linux as on a Mac, for
Android and the Android and desktop targets of Compose Multiplatform; iOS targets are skipped.
Installs with Homebrew, a `.deb` or an `.rpm`. See [[Installation]].

## v0.7.0 · Flutter

Flutter widget `@Preview`s on iPhones, iPads and Android devices, every language and appearance,
on a Mac or Linux. On a Mac with Xcode, iOS renders on Flutter's iOS engine, pixel identical to a
booted simulator. See [[Flutter]].

## v0.8.0 · Migration from Paparazzi and Roborazzi

`swiftshot init` finds Paparazzi and Roborazzi setups, reads the device and settings of each test
and writes a `swiftshot.json` that renders each tested preview the same way. Nothing is removed
from the project, and a report lists what isn't covered. See [[Migrating|Migrating-from-fastlane]].

## v1.0.0 · Baseline comparison

Verify screenshots against a committed baseline, with an HTML diff report and a way to accept
changes on CI. Works on GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Bitrise, Codemagic and others. The first
baseline comes from CI, not from Paparazzi or Roborazzi images.

IDE plugins are no longer planned.
